quote: Stelle die Bedingung dafür auf, dass er auch noch für $f(x)=\sin(n+1)x, \cos(n+1)x, \dots$ genau ist.
english: Set up the condition for it to be exact also for f(x) = sin(n+1)x, cos(n+1)x, ...
topic: A quadrature problem: choosing nodes alpha_i so that an approximation of the integral of f from 0 to 1, exact for trigonometric combinations up to order n, is also exact for sin(n+1)x, cos(n+1)x, ..., by analogy with Gauss and Jacobi quadrature for polynomials.

triage.modern_statement: Trigonometric Gaussian quadrature. Take a rule Q(f) = Σ_{i=1}^{m} w_i f(α_i) for ∫_0^1 f(x) dx that is exact on trigonometric polynomials up to degree n, meaning the span of 1, cos kx, sin kx for k ≤ n. The question is how to choose the free nodes α_i, and what conditions they must satisfy, so that the rule is also exact for sin(n+1)x, cos(n+1)x and further higher harmonics. This is the trigonometric version of Gauss and Jacobi quadrature: the aim is maximal trigonometric degree of exactness for a given number of nodes. Because Hilbert's interval [0,1] is shorter than the period 2π, this is the 'subperiodic' case. On a full period the answer is the classical one: equally spaced nodes (the trapezoidal rule) are optimal.
triage.answered_by: There is no single answer to Hilbert's note itself, and I found no evidence that Hilbert published it. The general question was developed later. A. H. Turetzkii (1959, Uchenye Zapiski; English translation in East J. Approx. 11 (2005)) introduced interpolatory trigonometric quadrature rules with maximal trigonometric degree of exactness. G. V. Milovanović, A. S. Cvetković and M. P. Stanić (2008 and later) built a theory of Gaussian-type rules from orthogonal trigonometric polynomials of semi-integer degree. G. Da Fies and M. Vianello (2012/2013) constructed Gaussian-type rules on subintervals of the period: n+1 angles with positive weights, exact for all trigonometric polynomials of degree ≤ n on intervals shorter than 2π. That last setting matches Hilbert's interval [0,1].

evidence.claim: In 1959 Turetzkii introduced quadrature rules with maximal (even) trigonometric degree of exactness. A recent Springer chapter surveys this line of work.

Turetzkii studied interpolatory rules ∫_0^{2π} f(x)w(x)dx ≈ Σ_{ν=0}^{2n} w_ν f(x_ν) that are exact for trigonometric polynomials of degree ≤ n. Milovanović et al. developed a special Gaussian rule for this setting.

Milovanović, Cvetković and Stanić showed that orthogonal trigonometric polynomials of semi-integer degree satisfy a five-term recurrence relation. They used them to build quadrature rules of Gaussian type, building on Turetzkii.

Da Fies and Vianello constructed a quadrature formula with n+1 angles and positive weights that is exact on the (2n+1)-dimensional space of trigonometric polynomials of degree ≤ n, on intervals shorter than 2π. On the full period the angles become n+1 equally spaced angles.

Later work builds on subperiodic trigonometric Gaussian quadrature, for example subperiodic trigonometric hyperinterpolation (2018, in the Ian Sloan 80th-birthday volume) and product Gaussian rules on circular lunes.

triage.why: The note asks for conditions on the nodes so that a trigonometric quadrature rule gains extra exactness, explicitly by analogy with Gauss and Jacobi quadrature. That is exactly the question of Gaussian rules with maximal trigonometric degree. It was settled by Turetzkii (1959) and by Milovanović–Cvetković–Stanić, whose rules use semi-integer orthogonal trigonometric polynomials. For a subinterval like [0,1] it was settled by Da Fies–Vianello (2012/13). The topic is still active: a 2025 Springer survey chapter and ongoing subperiodic quadrature work exist. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem, and I found no source linking it to Hilbert. Confidence is medium rather than high because the note is short. In particular, the number of nodes Hilbert intended and his exact form of the rule are not stated, so it can't be confirmed that his precise formulation matches these results one-to-one.
